The truth is that if an idea is important, it’ll come back to you. It’ll be so strong that you’ll remember it. You’ll find yourself thinking about it again and again. And if it’s not, then it’s probably not a big deal to let it go.
This applies to more than just writing. If you forget to buy your partner a gift, that’s a problem. If you forget to send a thank-you email to a colleague, that’s also a problem. But if you forget to check out a new coffee shop that you only heard about once, that’s probably not a big deal.
The important things will come back to you. Trust that. Don’t stress about the little things.

### Title: Engaged

### Content: 
The word “engaged” means a lot of things. For one, it means “busy.” “Occupied.” “Already in use.” By the time you agree to marry someone, that sure will be the case. You’ll already have seen your fair share of love. With each other. With the others. But now, you agree to hold out for someone special, and, in the meantime, no one else shall take that special place.
To be engaged, however, also means to be “involved.” “Interested.” “Committed.” The more you engage with something, the more you’ll care about it. The more you’ll be willing to give it your time, attention, and energy. That, too, is what we want from our relationships. We want our partner to care about us. To be involved in our lives. To be committed to the relationship.
Finally, to be engaged means to be “in combat.” “In battle.” “In the fight.” And that’s the part we often forget. It’s not just a fight for our partner’s attention, love, and affection. It’s also a fight for our own. A fight against our ego. Our desire to be right. Our fear of being wrong. Our lack of patience. Our need for control. Our urge to run away when the going gets tough.
Love is a fight for what’s good, true, and beautiful. It is a fight against what’s bad, false, and ugly. And it is a fight we must all engage in if we ever hope to win it.
Love is the fight of our lives, and the only way to win is to be engaged.

### Title: The Kind of Letter You Want To Receive

### Content: 
“Maybe we are both idiots?” The words were staring back at me from a postcard. The paper was printed in Italy, but it was written on in German—by a guy in Poland, naturally. My friend Robert—aka Multithink —truly lives up to his online alias.
Robert like-minded people. He knows people from all over the world. He’s been to many places, and he has a knack for making friends wherever he goes. He’s also a big believer in serendipity. That’s why he sends postcards to people he knows will appreciate them. It’s a habit he’s had for years, and it’s a beautiful one.
He never knows when or where a postcard will arrive, but when it does, it’s always a pleasant surprise. “Maybe we are both idiots?” I guess I am. I’ve known Robert for a long time. I’ve been to his house. I’ve met his parents. We’ve had long discussions about philosophy, history, and, of course, the meaning of life.
The postcard was a follow-up to a recent conversation we’d had. “I’m still thinking about what you said,” I told him. “I’m not sure I have an answer yet, but I think I have a question.” That question was: “Maybe we are both idiots?”
The question was about a specific topic, but it could also be applied to life in general. “Maybe we’re all idiots?” I don’t know. But I do know that, when it comes to sending postcards, Robert is no idiot at all.
He’s a man who understands the value of human connection. He knows that a simple gesture can go a long way. And he’s not afraid to show his appreciation for the people in his life.
That’s the kind of person I want to be. The kind of person who sends postcards. The kind of person who makes an effort to stay in touch. The kind of person who values human connection.
And that’s the kind of letter I want to receive. A letter from a friend, written with sincerity and sent with love. A letter that says, “I’m thinking of you.” A letter that says, “I care about you.” A letter that says, “Maybe we are both idiots?”
Because, at the end of the day, we are all idiots. We’re all trying to figure out this thing called life. And we’re all doing the best we can.
So, the next time you receive a postcard in the mail, don’t just throw it away. Read it. Appreciate it. And remember that there’s someone out there who cares about you.
Maybe we are all idiots. But we’re all in this together. And that’s worth a lot more than any postcard could ever say.

### Title: Tainted Material

### Content: 
Despite recently descaling our electric kettle, its filter kept clogging up. After each boil, the hot water would only drizzle out in spurts. “What’s with this thing?” I thought, “I just cleaned it!” I took out the filter at the spout, rubbed it, shook it, and put it back.
The next time I used the kettle, the water was back to normal. “That’s weird,” I thought. “What did I do?” I realized I had taken out the filter twice, but the second time, I had turned it around. The side that was facing the spout was now facing the inside of the kettle. “Huh. Maybe that did the trick.”
I tried it again, and sure enough, the filter worked better when I turned it around. “But why?” I wondered. I took out the filter and looked at it. It was dirty. “Oh! The other side is dirty. That’s why it works better.” It seems the filter is made of two materials: a stainless steel mesh and a plastic frame. The plastic frame is the part that gets dirty, and the stainless steel mesh is the part that filters the water.
The plastic frame is a tainted material. It’s not part of the solution. It’s part of the problem. The plastic frame is there only to hold the mesh in place, but it also prevents the mesh from doing its job. The mesh can’t be removed from the plastic frame, so the only way to keep the kettle working is to turn the filter around every once in a while.
The next time you’re struggling with a tool, ask yourself: “Am I using tainted material?” If the answer is yes, you might be able to flip the problem on its head — and the result will be as clear as a cup of hot water.

### Title: The Perfect, Imperfect Filter

### Content: 
In the two and a half hours we hung out, Michael and I talked about everything under the sun: work, blockchain, productivity, parenting, self-care, writing, creativity, and on and on. One particularly noteworthy topic? Note-taking.
Michael is a big fan of Roam Research. He thinks it’s the best note-taking tool out there. I’m a big fan of Evernote. I think it’s the best note-taking tool out there. We debated for a good while. We both made good points. In the end, however, we agreed: There is no perfect note-taking tool. Not for everyone, and not at all times.
I’m an Evernote fan because it’s been around forever, and it’s just a simple, reliable, always-syncing note-taking tool. I like to keep my notes in folders, and I like that I can access them from any device at any time. Michael, meanwhile, prefers Roam because it allows him to link notes to one another and create a big web of ideas. He can see how his thinking is connected and how ideas relate to one another.
The truth is that both tools are great, and both tools are flawed. There is no perfect note-taking tool because there is no perfect note-taker. Everyone takes notes differently, and no tool can ever capture all the idiosyncrasies of human thinking in one system. The perfect note-taking tool would be a perfect AI that would read your mind and file away your thoughts in real-time. Until we have that, we’ll have to make do with what we have — and that’s perfectly fine.
The best you can do is to find the tool that works for you right now. That’ll be the perfect, imperfect filter. You’ll use it until it no longer works, and then you’ll switch to something else. That’s how life is. There is no perfect anything, and no perfect person, but there are perfect moments — and those are the ones we should savor.
Enjoy your note-taking tool. Enjoy your partner. Enjoy your job. Enjoy the moment. Don’t let the imperfections keep you from doing what you’re meant to do — and that’s to live life to the fullest.

### Title: If You Want To Break Something, Use a Hammer

### Content: 
The Green Hornet is a superhero who’s been reinterpreted many times since his invention in 1936. Similar to Batman, he’s a wealthy publisher who fights crime as a masked vigilante at night. In a 1966 TV show edition, his sidekick and loyal driver, Kato, received a significant upgraded to his previously only alluded to martial arts skills. Why? Bruce Lee played the part.
Despite’t having much screen time, Kato was a hit. He was mysterious, smart, and, most importantly, a kick-ass fighter. In the 2011 remake, Kato is played by Jay Chou, but the fighting skills are still there. In one scene, he and The Green Hornet find themselves in a warehouse, surrounded by bad guys. As Kato starts to kick some serious butt, his boss asks him what he’s doing. Kato’s response is classic:
“If you want to break something, use a hammer.”
It’s a bit like the saying “if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail,” but with a twist: if you want to build a house, use a hammer. If you want to break something, use a hammer. In other words, don’t use a screwdriver when you need a hammer. Pick the right tool for the job.
The same applies to our lives. If you want to write a book, use a pen. If you want to build a company, use a computer. If you want to become a chef, use a knife. There are a million ways to spend your time, but only a few of them will lead you to your goals.
Don’t be like The Green Hornet, trying to fight with his bare hands. Be like Kato. Be the one who shows up with the hammer.

### Title: Working Titles

### Content: 
Every time I see the words on the big screen again, I marvel at the brilliance behind the name: “a Working Title production.” Working Title is one of Britain’s most successful movie studios ever, the company behind films like Love Actually, Darkest Hour, and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, among many others. Making their own name one that would forever remain in progress didn’t just make for great marketing. It’s also a good reminder there’s always work left to be done.
When I first started writing, I was obsessed with titles. I’d spend hours trying to come up with the perfect one. Now, I almost always just write “Working Title” and get on with the show. It’s a much better use of time. Plus, it makes it easier to come up with a good title later. The first idea is rarely the best one, but it’s often the hardest one to find.
Working titles are a great way to keep going when you’re stuck. “Working Title” is also a great reminder that you’re always working. Whether it’s on your title, your latest project, or the next one in line, there’s always something to do — and that’s a good thing.
Working Title is a great name for a movie studio, but it’s also a great name for a human being. We’re all working titles, and we’ll never stop working.

### Title: What Are We Doing?

### Content: 
It’s a question that deserves asking. And often. Today at work, four people were discussing the specifics of a video I didn’t know we were creating, nor what for. So I asked: “What are we doing here?” No one had an answer, and if nothing else, it showed us: Perhaps we are trying to do too much.
My girlfriend and I had a similar conversation this week. “Why do we have to do so much? Why can’t we just enjoy the little things?” We’ve been together for seven years, and in that time, we’ve had some great adventures, but we’ve also spent a lot of time at home, cooking, reading, watching movies, and just talking. Those times were some of our best times.
It’s easy to get carried away. To go, go, go. To do, do, do. But it’s rarely the doing that matters. It’s the being. The people we’re with. The memories we make. Those memories can be made in a million different ways, and not all of them require grand gestures.
Don’t forget to ask: What are we doing? You might not always get an answer, but you’ll always get a chance to reflect — and perhaps remember that, actually, what we’re doing is just fine.

### Title: Keep Your Cool

### Content: 
Talking about not freaking out during major stock market declines in his 2017 annual shareholder letter, Warren Buffett suggested we remember a few select lines from a 19th-century poem by Rudyard Kipling, If :
“If when you’re feeling troubled
And you feel that you’ve been double-crossed
Just remember that you’re the one
Who can fill your mind with lots of thoughts
You can do what’s right or wrong
You can be weak or you can be strong
But I know you’ll make up your mind
The poem is a guide to keeping your cool. To staying calm and collected in the face of adversity. That’s what it’s about.
And while, yes, that’s a great attitude to have when your portfolio is down 30%, it is also the right mindset for any time. Not just the tough ones. It is a mindset for life.
“Don’t let the noise of others’ opinions drown out your own inner voice,” Steve Jobs once said. “And most important, have the courage to follow your heart and intuition. They somehow already know what you truly want to become. Everything else is secondary.”
You can choose to follow your heart. You can choose to ignore the noise. You can choose to not let others’ opinions drown out your inner voice. That’s what the poem is about. That’s what it’s always been about.
In the poem, Kipling addresses his son. But it’s really about anyone. About all of us. It’s about being a good person. A person of virtue. A person who keeps their cool. That’s what it’s about.
“Or walk with Kings—nor lose the common touch,” Kipling writes. “If all men count with you, but none too much.” It’s about being a good person. A person of virtue. A person who keeps their cool.
And you can choose to be that person. You can choose to keep your cool. You can choose to be a person of virtue. You can choose to be a good person.
You can choose to be the person you were meant to be. And you can choose to do it every single day. That’s what the poem is about. That’s what it’s always been about.
“If you can keep your head when all about you
Are losing theirs and blaming it on you,
If you can trust yourself when all men doubt you,
But make allowance for their doubting too;
If you can wait and not be tired by waiting,
Or being lied about, don’t deal in lies,
Or being hated, don’t give way to hating,
And yet don’t look too good, nor talk too wise:
If you can dream—and not make dreams your master;
If you can think—and not make thoughts your aim;
If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster
And treat those two impostors just the same;
If you can bear to hear the truth you’ve spoken
Twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools,
Or watch the things you gave your life to, broken,
And stoop and build ’em up with worn-out tools:
If you can make one heap of all your winnings
And risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss,
And lose, and start again at your beginnings
And never breathe a word about your loss;
If you can force your heart and nerve and sinew
To serve your turn long after they are gone,
And so hold on when there is nothing in you
Except the Will which says to them: ‘Hold on!’
If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue,
Or walk with Kings—nor lose the common touch,
If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you,
If all men count with you, but none too much;
If you can fill the unforgiving minute
With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run,
Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it,
And—which is more—you’ll be a Man, my son!”

### Title: Improving Without Criticism

### Content: 
George Lee may not have been part of Bruce Lee’s bloodline, but he was definitely family. As Bruce’s equipment manager—and, more importantly, maker —he forged dozens of specialized training items based on Bruce’s ideas and requests.
As a result, Bruce would often visit George’s workshop in the early morning, and the two would talk shop. One day, Bruce asked George why he didn’t take any notes. George said he had a good memory. “But how do you remember the mistakes?” Bruce asked. “If you don’t write down your mistakes, you can’t correct them.”
George shrugged. “You’re right. I’ll start writing things down.” Bruce smiled and left. The next day, he returned with a gift: a little book, titled “George’s Little Green Book.” “This is where you write down your mistakes,” Bruce said.
George was happy to receive the gift, but he didn’t expect what came next: Bruce handed him a second book. “This is where you write down my mistakes,” he said. “When I make a mistake, I want you to write it down in this book.”
George was stunned. “Bruce, why do you want me to write down your mistakes?”
“Because I don’t want you to make the same mistakes I make,” Bruce said. “I want you to be better than me.”
George was speechless. “I don’t know what to say.”
Bruce smiled. “Then don’t say anything. Just write.”
We can’t always offer criticism in the moment, but that doesn’t mean we can’t offer it at all. Don’t wait for the perfect moment. Make the moment perfect. It’s never too late to hand someone a little green book.
Even better, however, is to ask them for one. “Here’s where I’ll write down my mistakes. Where’s the one where you write down mine?”
Improvement is a two-way street, and there’s no reason why we can’t both benefit from each other’s mistakes.

### Title: Knowing Too Much and Too Little

### Content: 
The more time he spends wandering through the Aiel Waste, a barren, desert landscape in the Wheel of Time universe, the more “Dragon Reborn” Rand al’Thor understands the extent of his powers. Powerful magic that’s bound to corrupt him, strength to withstand even strong enemies’ attacks, and unreliable but enlightening visions of the future—such are the burdens of the chosen one.
As he continues to learn about his abilities, however, Rand also realizes how much he doesn’t know. “I have to know more,” he tells his friend Mat. “I have to learn…”
“Learn what?” Mat says. “How to fly? How to be safe from Aes Sedai and the Forsaken? How to win the Last Battle? Light, Rand, you are the Dragon Reborn! You are what you are. Learn to live with it!”
It’s true. Rand is the Dragon Reborn, and there’s nothing he can do to change that. But it’s also true that the more he learns, the better he can handle this fact—and all the responsibilities that come with it.
It’s a classic case of knowing too much and too little at the same time, and we all face it. The more we know, the more we realize we don’t know. The more we understand, the more we see what we’ve misunderstood. And the more we do, the more we’ll see how much we have yet to do.
In that sense, we are all the Dragon Reborn. We have to learn to live with what we are, but we also have to keep learning in order to do so. It’s a never-ending cycle, and while we can’t do anything to stop it, we can choose to accept it.
Don’t worry about knowing too much and too little. Just keep learning, and you’ll always know enough to do what’s right.
